Reviewer 3 (MB): Basal cell carcinoma is treated first line with surgical removal, which has an approximately 99% cure rate, while Hedgehog pathway inhibitors (HPIs) are reserved for the rare advanced cases where surgery is not feasible. In those settings, HPIs produce response rates of roughly 40–60%, and many patients experience meaningful tumor shrinkage or disease stabilization, but complete cures are less common than with surgery and tumors may recur after treatment stops. Their utility is further limited by acquired resistance, often through SMO mutations or downstream pathway activation such as GLI, as well as by a distinct toxicity burden that includes muscle cramps, alopecia, dysgeusia, weight loss, and fatigue; they are also teratogenic, requiring strict pregnancy prevention, and long-term tolerability is often poor enough that many patients discontinue therapy. A local injection approach could potentially reduce systemic side effects, but it is unlikely to replace surgery and, even if priced competitively with HPIs, would probably address only a very small commercial market.

MAGL (Monoacylglycerol lipase) inhibitors are a niche but increasingly interesting class of drugs that sit at the intersection of lipid metabolism, immunology, and cannabinoid biology. MAGL is an enzyme that: (i) breaks down 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG), a key endocannabinoid and (ii) generates arachidonic acid, a precursor for pro-inflammatory eicosanoids. Net (positive) effects can be: anti-inflammatory, nalgesic and neuroprotective. There is strong scientific rationale (from literature). I assume the p in pMAGLi stands for peripheral restricted.
